title: Is the BeagleY-AI, BeagleBoard.org's Linux board with TI's AM67A, the right board for a vision project?
short: The BeagleY-AI is a Linux board from BeagleBoard.org (not TI) built around TI's AM67A: four Cortex-A53 cores at 1.4 GHz, a 4 TOPS C7x accelerator, 4 GB of RAM and a hardware H.264 and H.265 codec. 11 precompiled zoo models ran on the accelerator in 5.4 to 49.1 ms; the pose model takes 43.1 ms there and 4.48 s on the Arm cores with two threads. Hardware decode of 1080p H.264 runs at 255.9 fps and hardware encode at 110.1 fps. TI's people-count demo ran at 28.0 to 29.4 fps from a USB webcam on a rated 5 V 3 A supply. These are one board's numbers, taken with no fan.

meet.what: A Linux board from BeagleBoard.org, not from TI, around TI's AM67A vision processor. The C7x is TI's DSP core and the MMA beside it is the matrix accelerator that runs neural nets; TIDL is TI's runtime that offloads a network to it; Wave5 is the video codec block. It runs BeagleBoard's Edge AI image (TI's Edge AI Linux release, built for this board) from a microSD card, and every run here went over Ethernet and ssh: no serial adapter, display or debug probe was needed. Ours is the 4 GB model. The USB-C port is power only on this image, and the board needs a 5 V 3 A supply that is not in the box.
facts: Four Cortex-A53 at up to 1.4 GHz, without ARMv8.1 atomics (a program built with them dies with Illegal instruction); R5F cores at up to 800 MHz (TI AM67A product page, read 2026-11-10)

Two C7x DSPs with MMA, up to 4 TOPS combined; both reported a 1.0 GHz clock on our board (k3conf). Hardware H.264 and H.265 encode and decode (Wave5), rated by TI up to 4K at 60 fps; GPU, IMG BXS-4-64 (TI AM67A product page; not tried here)
4 GB LPDDR4; Linux on this image sees 2,529 MB, the rest is reserved for the accelerators and firmware; no swap
microSD only; a 128 GB card gave a 119 GB root partition

Gigabit Ethernet (used for every run), four USB 3.0 Type-A host ports (a USB webcam), one USB-C port (power only on this image), micro-HDMI, two MIPI CSI camera connectors, a 40-pin header, a 4-pin fan connector (BeagleBoard.org, read 2026-11-10). We did not use HDMI, the CSI cameras or the header
Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth LE 5.4 on a BM3301 module (TI CC3301); not used in any run
None used. The JTAG pads (Tag-Connect) and a 3-pin debug UART exist; we reached the board over Ethernet and ssh as root with no password

BeagleBoard Edge AI image 11.00.00.08 (built 2025-09-06): Arago 2025.01, Linux 6.12.33, GCC 13.3.0, Python 3.12.9, onnxruntime 1.15.0 with the TIDL provider, GStreamer, FFmpeg, Docker; no libc.a, no KVM
USB-C, 5 V at 3 A; the board does no USB-PD negotiation (BeagleBoard.org). A wall supply of unread rating let the board reboot under the camera demo; a rated 5 V 3 A supply did not

projects.t: Get Linux running from the box
projects.result: Edge AI image 11.00.00.08 written to a microSD card from a Mac (the card-write script needed two fixes first: the Mac's built-in SD reader lists the card as an internal disk, and a raw write must end on a whole 512-byte sector), then ssh as root with no password over Ethernet on first boot, 2026-11-03. The time from box to login was not recorded

projects.t: TI's model zoo on the C7x accelerator
projects.result: 11 of the 14 model folders ran on the accelerator, 5.42 to 49.09 ms each; the pose model took 43.13 ms with 274 of 274 nodes offloaded. The 8 models also run on the Arm cores (2 threads) took 15 to 111 times longer (pose 4,475.57 ms). The other 3 folders were not run. Against the SK-TDA4VM the same models were 2 to 4 times slower

Through GStreamer: H.264 decode of 1080p at 255.9 fps using 27 to 29 percent of the four cores' time (47.1 fps in software), H.264 encode at 110.1 fps, decode chained into encode at 135.1 fps. Decode into a program needs the frame scaled before it is converted (76.5 fps, against 6.5 fps the other way round). FFmpeg's hardware encoder hung and its decode into a pipe stopped after 3 frames

projects.t: Camera people count with TI's Edge AI demo
projects.result: On a rated 5 V 3 A supply the detector ran at 28.0 to 29.4 fps from a USB webcam at 720p, 5 of 5 starts held 60 s, and 29.7 fps for 60 s from a network camera; on a recorded clip 30.0 fps. On the earlier wall supply 0 of 5 camera starts held 15 s and the board rebooted (cause suspected to be the supply, not measured). No person has been counted from a camera: the on-screen count was 0 because the camera faced the bench

projects.t: Frigate object detection on the C7x
projects.result: Frigate 0.18.2 sent its detections to a 100-line server running the zoo's YOLOX-nano on the C7x: 64.46 ms per detection against 184.56 ms on Frigate's own CPU detector (a different, smaller model), tracking two people and a dog in a recorded clip. On a rated supply it ran 130 s each from the USB webcam (59.71 ms per detection) and from a network camera (58.01 ms) and detected nobody, because no person was in view. On 2026-11-03 Frigate's ffmpeg dropped the webcam off USB in 2 of 2 tries

projects.t: The Pop the bubbles pose game
projects.result: Pose on the C7x drove the game at 29.8 draw frames a second from the USB webcam for 20 s, and in a browser on a rated 5 V 3 A supply it held 60 s at 24.0 fps median (15.4 to 25.2). From a recorded clip at 1280x720 the first run drew 6.3 fps until background caching raised it to 20.6 fps; JPEG encoding for the browser is the remaining limit

projects.t: A language model and speech to text on the Arm cores
projects.result: llama.cpp v0.8.0 with Qwen2.5 0.5B Q4_K_M generated 6.87 tokens/s (1.5B: 2.42); whisper.cpp v1.9.5 tiny.en ran at 0.66 to 0.90 times real time and base.en at 1.32 on a 54 s clip. Neither uses the C7x

Home Assistant answered over HTTP 52.7 s after start (container 531 MB); Mosquitto was ready in 3.4 s; Pi-hole needed FTLCONF_dns_listeningMode=BIND because systemd-resolved holds port 53, then answered in 12.2 s

projects.t: One portable C app on Linux and on the MCU R5F core
projects.result: The AM62L's 66-line Linux glue file built byte-identical with the board's own gcc (2.288 s) and printed 14 lines a second apart, with a 2-line config header. A Zephyr build of the same app (21,372 bytes) loaded onto the MCU R5F core from Linux and printed 16 lines at 1.00 s gaps. The board has no ADC, so every line read 65535, and the LED was not seen

chains.t: Working with no display, serial adapter or probe
chains.why: Every run went over Ethernet and ssh as root. The one thing to know: the USB-C port is power only, so it never shows up as a network adapter

chains.verdict: Not through FFmpeg, yes through GStreamer
chains.why: FFmpeg's h264_v4l2m2m encode never finished (the kernel printed result not ready: 0x800) and decode into a pipe stopped after 3 frames; GStreamer's v4l2h264enc and v4l2h264dec worked

chains.t: A USB webcam on a board fed from a hub port
chains.verdict: Only on a rated 5 V 3 A supply
chains.why: The Insta360 Link 2 Pro dropped off USB at 1080p 7 of 7 times and after gimbal moves; on a rated 5 V 3 A supply it held at 720p in five 60 s starts

chains.t: Compiling our own models for the C7x
chains.why: All 11 models used TI's precompiled artifacts from /opt/model_zoo; TI's compilation tools were not tried on this board

chains.t: Display, audio, the 40-pin header, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, the GPU
chains.why: Nothing was attached or tried: no display, no audio device and nothing on the header or the radio module

good_for: Camera and vision projects that need a neural net at video rate on a small Linux board: the zoo models ran on the accelerator in 5.4 to 49.1 ms, and the people-count demo held 28 fps from a webcam
Hardware video through GStreamer: 1080p decode at 255.9 fps and encode at 110.1 fps
Moving code between boards: the AM62L's Linux glue file built here unchanged, and the same app ran on the MCU R5F core
not_for: A bench with no 5 V 3 A USB-C supply: the board needs one, does not negotiate USB-PD, and rebooted under the camera demo on a supply of unread rating
FFmpeg-based video pipelines: its hardware encoder hung and its decode into a pipe stopped; plan on GStreamer
Sustained runs without a fan: the board read 70 to 87 degrees C in our runs with the fan connector empty, and no temperature log was kept
Microcontroller-style analog work: there is no ADC on the board, and no debug probe for the cores
Judging the chip's ceiling from this page: one board, one image, no fan, and the accelerator is a 4 TOPS part, about half the SK-TDA4VM's
buy: Made by BeagleBoard.org and not sold on TI.com; the maker's page is beagleboard.org/boards/beagley-ai. In the box: the board with its antenna and a quick-start card. Not in the box: a 5 V 3 A USB-C supply, a USB-C to USB-C cable, a microSD card, a micro-HDMI cable (BeagleBoard.org documentation, read 2026-11-01).
gotchas: The board is powered from your computer's USB-C port but never shows up as a network adapter
Reach it over Ethernet. On the Edge AI image the USB-C port carries power only; find the address in your network's client list (host name j722s-evm)
The Mac refuses the card, or a raw write ends with an error

Use beagley-ai/tools/write-card.sh: it accepts the Mac's built-in SD slot (which lists as an internal disk) and pads the image to whole 512-byte sectors. A full card write with the current version has not been run
A model load never returns and the next ones hang too
Reboot the board and run one model per process with a timeout. Seen once; no log of the hang was kept and the cause is unknown
Pose takes 43 ms where 25 to 30 ms was expected

Nothing is wrong (the 25 to 30 ms was our guess from the SK-TDA4VM's 13.76 ms and its 8 against 4 TOPS): every one of the model's 274 nodes runs on the accelerator, and TI's datasheet figures for two other models are near what we measured, about 19 percent slower by the timing used here
FFmpeg hardware encode never finishes, or decode into a pipe stops after 3 frames
Use GStreamer: v4l2h264enc for encode, and for decode into a program scale the frame before converting it
TI's camera demo runs at 1 fps with the C7x idle
Set SOC=j722s in the environment; a login shell sets it and a plain ssh command does not, and the app then runs the model on the Arm cores
The board leaves Ethernet and reboots seconds after the camera demo starts
Power it from a rated 5 V 3 A USB-C supply. On a wall supply of unread rating 4 of 5 starts rebooted within 15 s; on a rated one 5 of 5 held 60 s. Cause suspected, not measured
A program dies with Illegal instruction
The Cortex-A53 has no ARMv8.1 atomics; preload the trap library from am62l-evm/steam/lse_trap/
The board reads 80 to 87 degrees C in long runs
The fan connector was empty; fit a fan before runs longer than a few minutes. No temperature log was kept
measured_on: Measured 2026-11-03 to 2026-11-08 on one BeagleY-AI 4 GB from an Apple Mac over Ethernet and ssh. BeagleBoard Edge AI image 11.00.00.08 (built 2025-09-06), Linux 6.12.33, GCC 13.3.0, onnxruntime 1.15.0, microSD boot, no fan, no display. The camera runs used an Insta360 Link 2 Pro; the first camera runs were on a wall supply of unread rating and the later ones on a rated 5 V 3 A supply, as stated per row.

next.title: What do I do first with the BeagleY-AI?
steps: Get a 5 V 3 A USB-C supply and a C-to-C cable; the board has no USB-PD and the box has neither.
Write BeagleBoard's Edge AI image to a 32 GB or larger microSD card with beagley-ai/tools/write-card.sh.
Plug in Ethernet, then power; find the board's address in your network's client list (host name j722s-evm) and ssh in as root, no password.
Run the pose model on the accelerator with beagley-ai/bench/zoo/zoo_bench.py (43.1 ms), then read the FAQ before any camera or video run.

runs_note: Most projects in this list are microcontroller projects, such as blinking a pin or reading an ADC. They do not map onto a Linux vision board, so they do not apply here. The board's own tests are in the benchmarks below and on the results page.
